can say whether it was ever on the shelf, was taken to the reading room, or went home in
somebody's bag by mistake, which has happened, exactly once, and was not found for a fortnight.

Pests and water are the two threats that arrive without warning. Sticky traps are checked monthly
and the count is written down, because a rising count is the only early signal of an infestation. The
water alarm under the strong room floor is tested on the first Saturday of each month, and the
person testing it signs the sheet on the door. An unsigned month is treated as an untested month,
whatever anyone remembers about it now.

Loans out of the building are rare and are approved only by the committee, in writing, for
exhibition by another archive or museum with its own strong room and its own insurance. A loan is
packed by two volunteers, photographed item by item before it leaves, and accompanied by a
condition report that the borrower countersigns on arrival. Nothing goes on loan to a private
individual, a shop window or a school display case, however worthy the occasion, because those are
the places from which things do not come back. The rule has been tested twice and has held both
times.

Schools and local groups visit several times a year, and a visit is prepared the week before by
pulling a small selection of robust, vivid material onto a table in the workroom rather than taking a
party into the strong room. Children handle facsimiles and look at originals. The selection is
different each time, chosen for the group, and returned to the shelves the same afternoon with the
strong room log completed as usual, school visit or no school visit, and the log initialled by both
volunteers.

Volunteers on the desk keep a running list of the questions they could not answer, with the
researcher's name and what was tried, and the list is read at each committee meeting. It is the
archive's best measure of what it lacks. A question that comes up three times in a year usually
means either that a collection is uncatalogued and therefore invisible, or that the town once had a
record it no longer has and the archive should be asking around for it before the last person who
remembers it is gone. It is also, quietly, the archive's whole collecting policy.

Digitisation is done for access and for insurance, in that order, and never as a substitute for keeping
the original. A scanned register lets a searcher read it at home and spares the original from
handling; it does not permit the original to be discarded, and any suggestion that it might is
referred to the committee with the founding minute attached. Scanning is therefore planned around

provenance.key:
and keeps the strong room log; the other stays in the room. The rule of two is not about suspicion. It
is about having someone free to answer a question, find a reference, or deal with a spill while the
other is out of the room with a box on the trolley and no hands free.

Researchers sign the visitors' book and fill in a request slip for each box they want to see. Slips are
kept for seven years. They are the only record of which material has been consulted, which is useful
when a box is later found damaged and essential when a depositor asks who has looked at their
family's papers. Slips are filed by date, not by name, so that a search for one box's history means
reading a year rather than a name, which is slower and a great deal more reliable.

Requests are fetched in the order they arrive, and no researcher may have more than three boxes
on the table at once. A fourth request waits until one of the three goes back. Photography by
researchers is permitted for private study without flash and without a tripod, and each photograph
is noted on the request slip by box and item. Photocopying is done by volunteers only, on the flat-
bed copier, and refused for anything bound, fragile, larger than the platen, or dated before 1900.

Enquiries by post and email are answered within a month, and the answer says either what was
found, what was looked at without success, or what would need to be looked at and roughly how
long that would take. The archive does not undertake research on a searcher's behalf beyond an
hour, but it will always say what it holds and let the searcher decide whether to come. A reply that
says only that the material may exist is not an answer to anything, and it is not sent.

Closed material is rare but real. Some deposits carry a closure period set by the depositor, and some
records, school registers and medical ledgers in particular, are closed under the archive's own rule
for the lifetime of the people named in them. Closed boxes are shelved separately, marked on the
outside, and listed in the catalogue with their opening date so that a searcher knows the material
exists and when it will open, and can plan a visit accordingly rather than making a wasted journey.
